lessons.t: Cost modelling: tokens, reasoning, tools and retries
lessons.html:
Chapter 1’s lab priced a single request. Real features cost more than that, and the gap is where budgets go wrong. The unit that matters is cost per successful task: everything spent to get one user one good outcome, including the attempts that failed.

ComponentDriverOften missed because
Uncached inputSystem prompt, tools, history, retrieved documentsHistory and tool results grow every turn
Cache writes and readsStable prefix reused across callsWrites cost more than plain input; reads far less
Output and thinkingAnswer length and reasoning budgetThinking tokens are billed as output and rarely shown in the product
Tool feesSearch, code execution, third-party APIsPriced per call, outside the token bill
Tool results as inputSearch results, file contents, API payloadsThey re-enter context and are re-sent on later steps
Supporting modelsEmbeddings, rerankers, guardrail classifiers, judgesSit in other teams’ budgets
Retries and failuresTimeouts, schema failures, abandoned agent runsLogged as errors and missed in cost reports
Human reviewApprovals, escalations, quality samplingBooked as headcount and left out of COGS

Tool fees are real money. As of October 2026, Anthropic’s API charges web search at $10 per 1,000 searches on top of the tokens the results add, and its pricing page lists a 1.1× multiplier for US-only inference. Data-residency and regional premiums like that are easy to leave out of a model.

Agents grow quadratically

An agent re-sends its whole context on every step. Take an illustrative 10-step run with an 8,000-token system prompt and tools, where each step adds 2,000 tokens of tool results. The final context is 26,000 tokens, but the run pays for 170,000 input tokens (8,000 × 10 plus 2,000 × (0 + 1 + … + 9)). Double the steps and input cost roughly quadruples. Caching the growing prefix recovers most of that, which is why cache hit rate belongs on the agent dashboard.

Failure is a cost

If an attempt costs $0.12 and succeeds 80% of the time, and failures are detected and retried, the expected cost per successful task is $0.12 ÷ 0.8 = $0.15 (illustrative). Failures that aren’t detected cost more, because someone downstream pays to fix them. A cheaper model with a lower success rate can raise cost per successful task.

Model the distribution

Averages hide the users who break your pricing. Pull per-user cost from traces (Chapter 10) and report the median, the 95th percentile and the top 1%. In most AI features the distribution has a long right tail: a few users run long sessions, big documents or agents in loops, and they cost many times the median. The p95 user is who your pricing has to survive.

One formula for the spec

Cost per successful task = (Σ token costs + tool fees + supporting model costs) per attempt × attempts per success + human review per task. Fill it in per feature, from traces, at the median and p95.

What changes for you

  • Put cost per successful task at median and p95 in every AI spec, next to the quality bar.
  • Ask finance and engineering to tag supporting models, tool fees and human review to the feature, so COGS is complete.
  • For agent features, require step caps and a cache hit rate target; both bound the quadratic term.

lessons.t: Bending the curve: routing, caching, batching and smaller models
lessons.html:
Once you can see cost per successful task, you can bend it. The levers are well known. The skill is the order you pull them in, and checking each against the eval so a saving doesn’t quietly cost quality.

LeverTypical effectWatch out for
Trim contextFewer input tokens on every callRemoving context the hard cases needed
Shorter outputsOutput is the most expensive token typeAnswers truncated or too terse to be useful
Thinking budgetLess reasoning on easy tasksAccuracy drops on multi-step cases
Prompt cachingCache reads at 10% of the input price or less on Anthropic’s API (as of October 2026)Writes cost 1.25× to 2× input; changing tools, thinking settings or the model invalidates the cache
Batch processing50% off input and output on Anthropic’s Batch API; other major providers offer similar discountsResults can take hours; only for work that can wait
Routing and cascadesEasy requests go to a cheaper tierSilent misses when the router or escalation signal is wrong (Chapter 10)
Smaller or distilled modelOften an order of magnitude cheaper per tokenLower success rate can raise cost per successful task
Code for deterministic stepsRemoves model calls entirelyNone, if the step really is deterministic
Fewer agent stepsCuts the quadratic input termLess exploration on genuinely hard tasks

A sensible order

  1. Remove waste. Unused tools in the definition list, stale history, retrieved chunks nobody cites, verbose output formats. This is free quality-neutral money in most first versions.
  2. Structure for caching. Stable material first, variable last, as in Chapter 4. A 5-minute cache write at 1.25× pays for itself after one read.
  3. Move offline work to batch. Nightly summaries, backfills, eval runs and enrichment jobs rarely need real-time answers.
  4. Route. Classify by difficulty and send each class to the cheapest model that passes its slice of the eval.
  5. Swap or distil models. Only once the above are done, because each swap is a release (Chapter 10, lesson 3).
  6. Fine-tune a small model. For narrow, high-volume, stable tasks with plenty of graded examples (Chapter 7). Budget the re-run when the next base model arrives.

Judge every lever at fixed quality

Report each optimisation as a pair: change in cost per successful task and change in eval pass rate. A 40% cost cut with a 3-point quality drop is a product decision, and the PM makes it, with the numbers on the table.

Two traps recur. The first is optimising cost per call while cost per task rises, because a cheaper model needs more turns or more retries. The second is breaking the cache with a harmless-looking change: reordering tools, injecting a timestamp near the top of the prompt, or toggling the thinking setting. Watch cache hit rate after every prompt change, the same way you watch the eval.

What changes for you

  • Ask for a cost roadmap with levers in this order, each with its expected saving and its eval result.
  • Make cache hit rate and cost per successful task standard metrics in prompt-change reviews.
  • Classify every workload as interactive or deferrable; deferrable work goes to batch by default.

lessons.t: Why AI gross margins sit below classic SaaS
lessons.html:
Classic SaaS has a near-zero marginal cost per user. Once the software is built, serving another seat costs a little hosting and support, which is why mature SaaS gross margins are high. AI features break that assumption. Every use buys inference, the bill scales with usage, and the heaviest users cost far more than the lightest.

Why margins sit lower

  • Inference is variable COGS. Tokens bought from a provider, or GPUs you run yourself, scale with every request.
  • Usage is skewed. A flat seat price averages across users whose costs differ by orders of magnitude.
  • Adverse selection. Unlimited plans attract the heaviest users, who are often the ones who would pay for more.
  • Work per task keeps growing. Reasoning models and agents use more tokens on longer tasks. Cursor gave this as the reason for its June 2025 pricing change.
  • Supplier pricing power. If you resell a frontier model, part of your margin is set by your provider’s price list.
  • Hidden COGS. Judges, guardrail models, evals and human review all scale with volume.

A worked example

Illustrative numbers. 100 users pay a $30 monthly seat, so revenue is $3,000. Monthly inference cost per user varies:

UsersCost eachTotalShare of inference cost
50 light$1$509%
40 regular$5$20035%
9 heavy$25$22540%
1 extreme$90$9016%
100$565100%

Inference is 19% of revenue, so gross margin before other COGS is about 81%. That looks healthy until you see that the top 10 users drive 56% of cost and one user costs three times their seat. If only the top 10 users double their usage, inference rises to about 29% of revenue. If a new feature doubles tokens per task for everyone, it reaches about 38%. The average looked fine; the tail sets the margin.

Treat margin statistics with suspicion

Figures for “typical AI company gross margins” circulate widely. Most come from small surveys or investor samples, with unclear definitions of COGS and no split between AI and non-AI revenue. Don’t anchor a pricing decision on them. Use your own trace-derived costs and your finance team’s COGS definition.

What protects margin

Usage allowances and fair-use limits on flat plans; tiers that put heavy users on higher prices; overage pricing at or above cost; routing and caching from lesson 2; and pricing on usage or outcomes where cost varies most (lesson 4). Each one shifts some of the variance from you to the customer, which affects how predictable their bill is. That trade is the core of AI pricing.

What changes for you

  • Show inference cost by user decile in the business review, alongside the blended margin.
  • Model margin under a doubling of heavy-user usage and of tokens per task before you set a flat price.
  • Ask where every margin benchmark in a deck came from, and replace it with your own numbers if the answer is vague.

lessons.t: Seats, usage, hybrid and outcome-based pricing
lessons.html:
There are four ways to charge for an AI feature, and most real price lists combine them. The choice decides who carries cost variance and how predictable the customer’s bill is.

ModelCustomer pays forWho carries cost varianceFits when
SeatAccess, per user per monthYouUsage is even across users and cost per user is low against the price
Usage or creditsRequests, tokens, actions or creditsCustomerCost varies widely and customers control volume
HybridSeat with an allowance, plus overageSharedMost users fit an allowance and a tail would wreck a flat price
OutcomeA defined result, such as a resolved conversationYou, per outcomeThe outcome is measurable, attributable and valued by the buyer

Real examples (as of October 2026)

  • Hybrid, with model multipliers. GitHub Copilot Pro is $10 a month with 300 premium requests, Pro+ is $39 with 1,500, and extra premium requests cost $0.04. Each model has a multiplier that sets how much of the allowance a request uses, so expensive models draw down faster.
  • A move from requests to usage. In June 2025 Cursor replaced request limits on its Pro plan with a monthly pool of usage at API rates. It apologised in July 2025 for poor communication and refunded unexpected charges. The model was defensible; the surprise wasn’t.
  • A menu of meters. Salesforce Agentforce lists $2 per conversation for customer-facing agents, Flex Credits at $500 per 100,000 credits (a standard action uses 20 credits, so $0.10), and per-user add-ons with unmetered employee use.
  • Per outcome. Intercom’s Fin charges $0.99 per outcome, where outcomes include a resolution (the customer confirms it helped or leaves without asking for more) and a successful procedure handoff, with at most one charge per conversation. Zendesk announced outcome-based pricing for its AI agents in August 2024, charging for automated resolutions. Sierra describes outcome-based pricing tied to results such as resolved conversations or saved cancellations, and doesn’t publish rates.

The hard part of outcome pricing

Outcome pricing aligns incentives and is easy to sell against headcount. It moves three problems onto you. Definition: a customer who leaves without replying might be satisfied or might have given up, and the contract has to say which counts. Attribution: when an AI agent and a human both touch a case, someone has to decide who resolved it. Variance: you’re paid per outcome but pay per token, so a hard month of long conversations comes out of your margin. Price it from your p95 cost per outcome, with a floor or minimum commitment.

A decision rule

If cost per user varies less than about 3× across users, a seat is simplest. If it varies more and customers control volume, meter it. Price on outcomes only when the outcome can be counted from logs both sides trust. These thresholds are judgement calls: test them on your own distribution.

What changes for you

  • Write the billing unit into the spec, with its exact definition and the log event that counts it.
  • Test every candidate price against median, p95 and top-1% cost per user before it goes to pricing committee.
  • Plan the customer’s view of usage (dashboards, alerts, caps) as part of the feature; Cursor’s episode shows the cost of surprise.

lessons.t: Planning for falling prices and rising usage
lessons.html:
Two trends pull in opposite directions. The price of a given level of capability falls fast. The amount of capability, and tokens, each task uses rises. Plan for both, or you’ll either overprice or lose money as the feature succeeds.

Prices for fixed capability fall fast

Epoch AI measured how quickly the price of reaching a fixed benchmark score fell. In its March 2025 analysis, the decline ranged from 9× to 900× per year depending on the milestone, and the price of matching GPT-4’s score on a PhD-level science benchmark fell about 40× per year. Epoch notes the fastest declines were recent, so it’s unclear they’ll persist. The durable lesson is direction and rough magnitude: last year’s frontier capability becomes cheap.

Spend per task often doesn’t fall

Your bill depends on which capability you buy and how much of it each task uses. Teams move to newer models as they ship. Reasoning models think longer on hard problems. Agents take more steps, read more files and run longer. Cheaper capability also invites more use: features that were too expensive get built, and users run them more often. Cost per task can rise even as price per unit of capability collapses.

Model three scenarios with illustrative factors applied to today’s cost per user:

ScenarioPrice per tokenTokens per taskTasks per userCost per user next year
Price wins× 0.3 (stay on a model that gets cheaper)× 1.2× 1.5× 0.54
Central× 0.5 (move to a newer tier)× 2× 1.5× 1.5
Usage wins× 0.8 (stay at the frontier)× 3× 2× 4.8

The point of the table is the spread. A plan that only assumes falling prices is a plan for the first row.

What to do with that uncertainty

  • Price on value. Cost-plus on today’s tokens ties your price to a number that will move a lot in both directions. Anchor price to the work the feature replaces or the outcome it produces.
  • Avoid unlimited promises. An unlimited plan is a bet on the first row. Use allowances and fair-use terms you can enforce.
  • Keep the option to switch models. Routing, an eval suite and a tested upgrade pipeline (Chapter 10) let you capture price drops quickly. Without them, falling prices don’t reach your margin.
  • Decide where savings go. Pass some to customers, keep some as margin, and spend some on quality, for example a bigger thinking budget on hard cases. Write that split down.
  • Re-forecast quarterly. Update the three scenarios from actual trace data, and review provider commitments and discounts at the same time.

The Chapter 13 link

Falling prices are a strategy question as well as a margin question. A feature that only works because a model is expensive to run elsewhere loses its edge when prices fall. Chapter 13, Strategy on a moving frontier, picks this up.

What changes for you

  • Replace the single cost forecast in your plan with three scenarios and the assumptions behind each.
  • Write a savings policy: what share of model price drops goes to price, margin and quality.
  • Add “can we switch models within a sprint?” to every AI feature’s launch checklist.

lab.title: Model cost per user and test three pricing models
lab.intro: You’ll build a cost distribution for one real feature from trace data and test three pricing models against it. The lab proves whether your intended price survives your heaviest users and next year’s usage.
steps: Pull 30 days of traces. For one live or beta feature, export per-task token counts (uncached input, cache reads and writes, output, thinking), tool calls and outcome. If the feature isn’t live, run 50 representative tasks from your eval set and extrapolate usage from a comparable feature.
Price every task. Apply your provider’s current rates, tool fees and any regional multiplier. Add supporting models (embeddings, guardrails, judges) and an estimate of human review per task.
Compute cost per successful task. Divide by the success rate from your Chapter 5 eval or online acceptance rate. Note the retry rate separately.
Build the user distribution. Aggregate to cost per user per month. Report median, p95 and top 1%, and the share of cost from the top 10% of users.

Test three pricing models. Pick a seat price, a hybrid (seat plus allowance plus overage) and a usage or outcome price. For each, compute gross margin on inference for the median user, the p95 user and the whole population.
Stress test. Rerun the three prices under the “Central” and “Usage wins” scenarios from lesson 5. Mark any price where p95 margin goes negative.
Pick and justify. Choose one model, state its billing unit and definition, and list the guardrails it needs (allowance, caps, fair use, minimum commitment).

quiz.q: A flat $25 seat looks profitable on average. Traces show the top 5% of users cost $60 a month each. What’s the best first move?
o: Raise the seat price for everyone
Add an allowance with overage or a higher tier, so the tail pays closer to its cost
Remove the feature for heavy users
Ignore it; averages are what matter
quiz.w: The tail sets the margin. An allowance or tier shifts variance to the users who create it without repricing everyone.

quiz.q: A team switches to a model with half the per-token price. Cost per successful task rises. What’s the likeliest reason?
o: The provider billed incorrectly
Caching stopped working permanently
The cheaper model succeeds less often or takes more turns, so retries and steps grow
Batch pricing was disabled
quiz.w: Cost per successful task divides by the success rate and multiplies by steps. A cheaper model that fails more can cost more per good outcome.

quiz.q: A 20-step agent re-sends its growing context on every step. Which change most directly limits its input cost?
o: Raising temperature
Shorter final answers
Moving the agent to a seat-based price
Caching the stable, growing prefix and capping steps
quiz.w: Input cost grows roughly with the square of steps. Caching the reused prefix and capping steps both bound that term.

quiz.q: You’re considering per-resolution pricing for a support agent. Which question matters most before launch?
o: Exactly what event in the logs counts as a resolution, and whether the customer agrees
Which model has the best benchmark score
Whether competitors charge per seat
How many tokens the system prompt uses
quiz.w: Outcome pricing lives or dies on a definition both sides trust. A customer who leaves silently might be satisfied or might have given up.

quiz.q: A deck claims “AI companies average X% gross margin” from an unnamed survey. How should you use it?
o: As the target for your pricing model
As a ceiling on your margin
Set it aside and use your own trace-derived costs and your finance team’s COGS definition
Average it with your own number
quiz.w: Third-party margin figures rarely define COGS or separate AI from non-AI revenue. Your own distribution is the only reliable basis.

quiz.q: Model prices for fixed capability are falling fast. Which planning assumption is safest?
o: Cost per user will fall at the same rate as prices
Cost per user could fall or rise depending on model choice, tokens per task and usage, so plan three scenarios
Prices will stop falling next year
Usage per user will stay constant
quiz.w: Falling unit prices are offset by newer models, longer reasoning and agent runs, and more use. Scenario planning captures the spread.

deliverable.title: Pricing and margin brief for one AI feature
deliverable.html:
A one-page brief for product, finance and sales leadership. Every number links to the sheet behind it.

  1. Feature and value. What it does, for whom, and the work or outcome it replaces.
  2. Cost per successful task. Median and p95, broken into tokens, tool fees, supporting models, retries and human review, with the date of the price list used.
  3. User distribution. Cost per user per month at median, p95 and top 1%, and the share of cost from the top 10%.
  4. Pricing options tested. Seat, hybrid and usage or outcome, with margin at median, p95 and population level.
  5. Recommendation. The chosen model, the exact billing unit and its definition, and the guardrails (allowances, caps, fair use, minimums).
  6. Scenarios. Margin under the three lesson 5 scenarios and the savings policy for price drops.
  7. Cost roadmap. The next three cost levers, expected savings and their eval results.
  8. Re-forecast trigger. When the brief must be redone: a provider price change, a model upgrade, or p95 cost moving more than an agreed amount.

Review it quarterly. Prices and usage both move faster than annual planning.
